title: Saying What Happened Without Naming the Doer

sections.title: No passive, three tools
sections.content: Hungarian has no everyday passive. When the doer is unknown, obvious or better left unnamed, news reports and workplace texts use one of three constructions. The active verb in the third person plural with no subject: *háromszáz dolgozót bocsátottak el* ('three hundred workers were laid off'), where 'they' means nobody in particular. A *-va/-ve* form with *van* for a resulting state: *a gyár kapui le vannak zárva* ('the factory gates are locked'). And, in official reports, *kerül* with a verbal noun in *-ra/-re*: *a túlórák kifizetésre kerültek* ('the overtime was paid'). That last one is correct but heavy.

sections.title: In labour news
rows: Three hundred workers were laid off.
Wages were frozen for a year.
A gyár kapui le vannak zárva.
A kollektív szerződés alá van írva.

sections.content: In the third-person-plural construction the thing affected stays the object, in the accusative: *a béreket befagyasztották*, not *a bérek befagyasztották*. Don't build an English-style passive with *lett* (*a sztrájk be lett tiltva*) in written Hungarian either: say *betiltották a sztrájkot*. If you do want to name the doer, make it the subject: *a vezetőség befagyasztotta a béreket*. For the *kerül* construction, most editors prefer the plain verb: *kifizették a túlórákat*.
